prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, and the first round has strengthened rather than weakened my view. The test I apply as an experimentalist is whether a result has been reproduced independently and whether the credited contribution was decisive. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once, and Ye's group took that concept to the most accurate and stable measurement ever made. JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others now operate lattice clocks and compare them, and Kroll's point that the 10^-18 level rests on systematic-shift budgets (blackbody, lattice light shift, collisions) cross-checked between laboratories is exactly the independent confirmation I look for. The new regime is concrete: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body clock physics, and the basis for the coming redefinition of the second. The credit is two names that appear identically on every ballot that includes the entry. Five of eight members prefer it, from different specialties, and no member has argued that it lacks maturity or credit clarity. I propose we draft the citation around the lattice concept and its record-level realisation, as Kroll, Olsson, Lindroth and Johansson each asked, and not around clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The serious objection, pressed by Danielsson and Eriksson, is that this is a refinement of metrology after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, and that the fundamental-physics payoff (drifting constants, dark matter, geodesy) is still largely prospective, with constant-variation results so far null, as Johansson and Lindroth note. I take that seriously, but it does not change my vote: the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct physical idea that changed the number of atoms and the stability regime, not a better version of the ion clock. The second reservation is credit. Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the concept and the accuracy evaluation, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. The three-person limit and the citation wording are the only tools we have, and the wording must claim no more than the concept and its first record-level realisations. Finally, I am an outsider to atomic physics, so my confidence in fine priority questions depends on Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson.

responses.point: His objection that the lattice clock is superb measurement science whose discovery content lies in instrumentation, with the fundamental-physics payoff mostly promised, and his statement that he would not oppose it and sees it as a fine second choice.
responses.response: I accept the premise that the payoff is partly prospective, but I do not think that makes it a lesser discovery. Before the lattice, spectroscopy of trapped atoms was limited by light shifts and small atom numbers. After it, thousands of atoms reach 10^-18 and clocks at different heights resolve the redshift over millimetres. That is a new observational window, opened by an instrument, which is the tradition in which this committee has worked. I am grateful that you would not oppose it. I also take your point about B004 seriously, and I have kept it as my first alternative, but I cannot defend a trio that leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp measured, and I think you concede the attribution gap yourself. I do not see a defensible three-name answer to my own chair's question for B004, so for me the decision is between a clean prize this year and a contested one.

responses.point: His preference for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, his argument that the cited discovery is the existence of the correlated phases and not their microscopic origin, and his admission that lattice clocks are unquestionably mature.
responses.response: The comparison with high-Tc superconductors is fair, and the continuum-theory prediction together with the 2018 experiments is a strong story. My difficulty is time and stability, not the quality of the physics. Eight years is short, Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and Cao have claims you accept are open, and the committee members closest to the field (Mehlig, Olsson, Johansson) all call it early, and Danielsson also judges it too young. I read your own statement that the clocks are unquestionably mature as the main point: when two criteria conflict, maturity and clean credit are the ones I weight most. I would not rule out B017 in a few years, and I would be glad to see it return, but I do not think a first-round preference from one member, even a well-argued one, outweighs the broad view that the interpretation is still moving.

responses.point: His position that the citation should name the concept and the first record-level realisations so as not to invite a priority argument, that the claim of new tests of fundamental physics should not lead because constants-variation results are null, and his disclosed proximity to circuit QED.
responses.response: I agree with this and I have adopted it. My revised citation leads with the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, and it leaves out the phrase about new tests of fundamental physics that you included in your round-1 wording, because null results should not be promoted into a headline. On circuit QED, I value your candour and I thank you for moving to B041 partly out of caution. I would still ask, as I did in round 1, that you not lead the committee's discussion of B028, but your technical input on what was decisive there remains welcome. Your point that a second prize part would push the union of names above three is correct, and it is one of my reasons for keeping the configuration to one part.

responses.point: His argument that the lattice clock is separated from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes by the magic-wavelength condition, that the 10^-18 level is verified by inter-laboratory comparison, and that the IceCube credit is hard to pin to two or three names.
responses.response: Your account of the systematic-shift budgets is the best answer to the 'single claim' worry, and I will use it in the committee's reasoning. I also accept your correction on IceCube. I ranked B029 second as a new window, but with a collaboration of roughly 300 people, TXS 0506+056 near three sigma, and the Galactic-plane and NGC 1068 results still recent, I cannot defend a cut at Halzen, Karle and Yoshida. That is why B029 stays an alternative and not a second part. I also note that you rank atom interferometry second, but I still think it should not be attached as a second part, since the Chu, Mlynek and Keith questions make that credit contested and a second part would break the three-person limit.

responses.point: His preference for KTHNY melting (B027) as a mature, analytically controlled theory with the three decisive authors, and his statement that he would accept B041 as the likely consensus.
responses.response: I respect the maturity of the KTHNY result and the clarity of its authorship, and I appreciate that you list B041 first among your alternatives. My question in round 1 was whether the hexatic phase was clearly confirmed experimentally and whether the 2016 citation left it uncovered. You concede overlap with the Kosterlitz-Thouless defect idea and first-order melting in hard-disk systems, and Danielsson and Eriksson are not persuaded. As a non-specialist I cannot adjudicate that, so I have to rely on the committee's overall pattern, in which no one else ranked it. Your request that the citation rest on the magic-wavelength mechanism and not on the record accuracy number is reasonable, and I have followed it.

responses.point: Her view that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice at the 10^-18 level, that Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko have claims on specific steps, and her suggestion that the secretary confirm that no recusal is needed for B002, B034 and B042.
responses.response: I agree on all three points. The citation names the lattice and the 10^-18 level, as your wording did. On Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko I think the committee should be honest in its own report that these are real contributions to the shift theory, early demonstrations and comparisons, and that the three-person limit is why they are not named, and not because the record is thin. As Chair, I will ask the secretary to confirm the recusal question you raise. I also note your own atomic-structure bias for B041, which you disclosed, and since Kroll and Olsson reached the same view independently from other specialities, I treat that bias as small.

uncertainties: Whether Danielsson and Eriksson, who prefer other candidates, will accept a precision-measurement prize this year, or will vote against it on novelty relative to 2005 and 2012.

Whether the committee's own wording can acknowledge Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups without implying that the prize leaves out the people who did the accuracy evaluation.
I rely on the atomic-physics members for priority details such as the first lattice-clock demonstrations and the current 10^-18 records, which I have not checked against sources.
Whether a defensible two- or three-person credit for IceCube or the GRB afterglows exists, since I could not find one, and so whether a second part is ever viable.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and in the same astroparticle community as IceCube and the GRB afterglow work (B029, B011), with no personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals. I have no tie to Katori, Ye or any B041 contributor. As Chair I treat my own preference as one view among eight, and I will ask the secretary to confirm Lindroth's recusal question. I also note Johansson's disclosed proximity to B028 and the other members' disclosures, none of which touches B041.
